title: Personalized functional networks scale with brain size beyond anatomy and are altered in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
authors: Sun, K. Y.; Snyder, W.; Tong, T. T.; Jaskir, M.; Sevchik, B. L.; Horien, C.; Jung, B.; Meisler, S. L.; Cieslak, M. L.; Prem, S.; Kafadar, E.; Gardner, M.; Hansen, J. Y.; Levitis, E.; Cyr, K.; Karandikar, S.; Seidlitz, J.; Bagautdinova, J.; Ruparel, K.; Li, H.; Fan, Y.; Shinohara, R. T.; Keller, A. S.; Raznahan, A.; Roalf, D. R.; Schmitt, J. E.; Gur, R.; McDonald-McGinn, D. M.; Gur, R.; Satterthwaite, T. D.; Alexander-Bloch, A. F.
abstract: Anatomically, cortical regions scale differentially with total brain size: some show disproportionate contraction in smaller brains and expansion in larger brains, while others show relative stability. Whether personalized functional networks (PFNs) follow similar areal scaling principles, and how these principles shape functional reorganization in conditions that alter brain size, remain unknown. We investigated PFN scaling in typical development (ages 8-23; n=1,332) and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a neuropsychiatric genetic disorder with globally reduced brain size (62 cases, 153 matched controls; ages 10-24). In typical development, PFN scaling diverged from anatomy, deviating more from proportional scaling, particularly in association networks. In 22q11DS, accounting for expected scaling with brain size reduction revealed two robust network effects: relative peripheral visual reduction and relative cingulo-opercular enlargement. Vertex-level 22q11DS PFN reorganization beyond global cortical reduction showed spatial alignment with normative PFN changes associated with brain size, linking typical scaling principles to disorder-related alterations.

title: Confidence in global motion discrimination is better predicted by perceptual reliability than by stimulus-based heuristics
authors: Oluk, C.; Szinte, M.; Masson, G. S.; Mamassian, P.
abstract: Decision-making requires evaluating the reliability of perceptual estimates, but whether confidence reflects perceptual reliability or stimulus-based heuristics remains debated. We used a multiple-aperture global motion stimulus in which the global direction, and therefore motion coherence, is only available after integrating locally ambiguous signals, so that no simple stimulus statistic can serve as a shortcut. Observers reported the global direction in two successive intervals and then chose which decision was more likely to be correct. Confidence tracked accuracy beyond what coherence alone could explain: observers were more accurate in chosen intervals even at the same coherence level. Observers also frequently reported the direction opposite to the true motion, and, in direct comparisons, were more confident in these errors than in other large errors. We compared two image-computable models of motion integration. A standard motion-energy model failed to produce opposite-direction errors and the associated confidence pattern. A normalized motion-energy model, adding tuned inhibition among direction channels and an untuned gain control that increases overall activation with coherence, accounted for most of the variance in both perceptual decisions and confidence judgments. Tuned inhibition, which must be sharp if it is close to excitation in strength, produced the opposite-direction errors and reproduced the direction of their confidence advantage, and the untuned gain was needed for confidence to depend on coherence as strongly as observed. Confidence was read out from the same signal as the perceptual decision, and noise at the confidence stage, although probably present, added little to the fit beyond explaining the accuracy difference between chosen and unchosen intervals. These results suggest that confidence in this task relies on perceptual reliability. They also suggest that seemingly unusual metacognitive behavior can emerge from perceptual computations, which must therefore be modeled explicitly to identify genuine confidence mechanisms.

title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
authors: Su, H.; Knight, C.; Liu, P. R.; Lee, H.
abstract: Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

title: From CSP7 to CSP5: Development of a soluble, truncated congener for the treatment of obstructive and restrictive lung diseases.
authors: Balnadupete, A.; Mugaranja, K.; Shetty, R.; Venkatesh, S.; Kumar, A.; Kleam, J. K.; Tang, H.; Peters, J.; Konduru, N.; Shetty, S.
abstract: Chronic obstructive and restrictive lung diseases (CLDs), represent a substantial worldwide health burden, with curative therapies remaining largely unavailable. Studies from our group and others have identified caveolin-1 (Cav1)-mediated signaling as a critical regulator of cellular processes implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of CLDs, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), silicosis and other progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PF) conditions. We have previously demonstrated that Cav1 scaffolding domain peptides (CSP and CSP7), attenuate lung injury and PF across multiple preclinical mouse models and exhibit protective and anti-fibrotic effects in COPD and IPF tissues ex vivo. The mechanism involves concurrent suppression of p53 and its downstream signaling in lung (airway and alveolar) epithelial cells by competitively counteracting excess Cav1, while restoring baseline p53 levels in (myo)fibroblasts persisting in fibrotic lungs, and alternatively polarized alveolar macrophages (AMs) by complementing Cav1 function. The safety and tolerability of inhaled micronized CSP7 dry powder (aka LTI-03), have been evaluated in mice, rats, dogs, followed by a Phase 1a clinical trial assessing safety and pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers (NCT04233814) and a Phase 1b trial in patients with IPF (NCT05954988). LTI-03 has subsequently advanced to a multicenter Phase 2 clinical trial in patients with IPF (NCT06968845). However, the FDA highlighted findings of minimal bronchiolar mucus cell metaplasia and hyperplasia in the 26-week rat inhalation study, raisings concerns regarding the suitability of poorly soluble CSP7 for long-term administration in patients with CLDs, particularly for COPD, a disease already characterized by goblet cell metaplasia and hyperplasia, mucus hypersecretion, impaired mucociliary clearance, and small airway obstruction. To address these limitations, we identified CSP5, a five amino acid truncated derivative of CSP7. Notably, the amorphous CSP5 attenuated p53 activation and apoptosis in preclinical models of tobacco smoke (TS)-, bleomycin, and silica-induced lung injury, demonstrating its potential to protect against epithelial injury across diverse lung disease models. Additionally, CSP5 enhanced surfactant protein C expression, consistent with alveolar epithelial cell homeostasis and regeneration, while suppressing Mucin 5Ac expression and attenuating distal lung injury in mice chronically exposed to TS. Furthermore, CSP5 promoted resolution of established PF in mouse models of bleomycin- or silica-induced fibrosis. CSP7, encompassing the CSP5 sequence, attenuates autophagic dysregulation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial membrane potential abnormalities, and mitochondrial superoxide production, and profibrotic polarization of AMs in mice with PF. Collectively, these findings position CSP5 as a formidable next-generation peptide with preserved bioactive motif of CSP7 while offering improved physicochemical and potential advantages in formulation flexibility. The dominant features of CSP5 support its further development for chronic inhaled or systemic administration in the treatment of obstructive or fibrotic lung diseases.

title: Docking and SPR identify candidate interactions between Apolipoprotein A-I and chemokine receptors
authors: Romel, C.; Blanchet, X.; Maas, S.; van der Vorst, E. P. C.
abstract: Background: Apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1), the main protein component of high-density lipoprotein, suppresses chemokine-driven leukocyte migration. This effect is usually attributed to indirect mechanisms such as cholesterol efflux, changes in lipid rafts, and altered receptor expression. Whether ApoA1 interacts with chemokine receptors directly is not known. Methods: We combined in silico rigid-body docking of AlphaFold-predicted structures (GRAMM-X, with interface analysis by PDBePISA) and surface plasmon resonance (SPR). In SPR experiments, ApoA1 was immobilized on the sensor, and CCR1, CCR5, CX3CR1, CXCR2, and CXCR4 were incorporated into proteoliposomes and injected as analytes. Mock proteoliposomes lacking any receptor served as a negative control. Kinetics were fitted with a 1:1 Langmuir model. Results: Docking predicted favorable interfaces between ApoA1 and all five receptors. CCR1 had the most favorable docking interaction, and CCR5 had the largest predicted interface (3716.7 A;iG -62.8 kcal/mol). Mock proteoliposomes showed no detectable binding to ApoA1, whereas all five receptors bound to ApoA1 in the SPR experiments. The apparent equilibrium dissociation constants (KD) were 3.44x10^-8 M for CXCR4, 3.96x10^-8 M for CXCR2, 5.26x10^-8 M for CCR5, 4.35x10^-7 M for CCR1, and 1.23x10^-6 M for CX3CR1. Conclusions: ApoA1 appears to bind chemokine receptors directly, with the highest apparent affinities for CXCR4, CXCR2, and CCR5. These findings suggest a candidate mechanism, complementary to cholesterol efflux and receptor expression regulation, by which ApoA1 may influence chemokine signaling. However, whether binding alters receptor signaling, internalization, or cell migration remains to be determined.

title: Pathogenic role of cGAS-STING pathway in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
authors: Rannou, A.; Manriquez, N.; Chakraborty, S.; Balaji, A.; Zarrow, J.; Alfaro, J.; Fournier, M.; Liu, W.; Kangavari, S.; Ibrahim, A.; Marban, E.; Rogers, R. G.
abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway is a critical component of the innate immune response to infection and cell stress. Chronic activation underlies human diseases such as lupus and inflammatory bowel disease, but cGAS-STING has not been implicated in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Compared to healthy controls, macrophages from DMD patients have high levels of cytosolic DNA and low levels of the DNA exonuclease, TREX1, a scavenger of cytosolic DNA upstream of cGAS-STING. Likewise, cytosolic DNA is elevated in macrophages from dystrophin-deficient mdx mice. Such macrophages over-produce cGAMP and secrete it locally, activating STING in neighboring myoblasts and thereby suppressing myogenesis. TY1, a synthetic non-coding RNA drug that enhances TREX1, attenuates cGAS-STING and restores cellular and tissue homeostasis in mdx mice. When administered intravenously or orally, TY1 not only halted disease progression but actually reversed cardiac and skeletal muscle pathology. Thus, pathological activation of cGAS-STING by cytosolic DNA mediates disease progression in DMD. Our work identifies TREX1, cGAS and STING as novel therapeutic targets in muscular dystrophy.

title: Spatial coordination of filamentous enzymes establishes a redox-balancing metabolon
authors: Kutlesic, N.; Krivitsky, S.; de Ruiter Swain, J.; Qiu, Y.; Yoon, S. J.; Yang, W.-H.; Pawlak, S.; Cifani, P.; Wee, T. L.; Lukey, M. J.
abstract: Nutrient scarcity in tumors prompts metabolic adaptations in cancer cells. Here, we identify that glutamine deprivation, a common feature of the tumor microenvironment, induces formation of a proline biosynthesis metabolon to selectively maintain intracellular proline levels. Mechanistically, filament-forming enzymes glutaminase (GLS) and pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS) co-assemble with the downstream reductases PYCR1 and PYCR2 into a physically associated enzyme complex within a spatially segregated mitochondrial subset. This assembly is dynamically regulated by the pathway intermediate glutamate and is membrane-anchored via ATP synthase. Disruption of enzyme spatial coordination compromises pathway activity, while the sustained proline biosynthesis is repurposed to support redox homeostasis under limited glutamine. We reveal nutrient-responsive filamentation and spatial coordination of mitochondrial enzymes as a mechanism of rapid metabolic adaptation to the fluctuating cellular environment.

title: Targeted siRNA screening coupled with unbiased proteomics identify potassium signaling as a critical regulator of pigmentation
authors: Ahuja, K.; Panthri, I.; Tanwar, A.; Jadon, A.; Biswas, A.; Maiti, T. K.; Motiani, R. K.
abstract: Ion channels are emerging as critical regulators of cellular signaling, influencing diverse pathophysiological processes and offering promising opportunities for therapeutic intervention. However, the contribution of ionic homeostasis to human skin pigmentation remains poorly understood. Here, we identify potassium (K+) dynamics as a critical regulator of pigmentation and uncover K+ channel Kir7.1 as a molecular link between K+ and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling. A targeted siRNA screen identified six previously unrecognized regulators of pigmentation, which we validated using mouse cell line systems, primary human melanocytes, and an in vivo zebrafish model. Unbiased proteomic analyses of two prominent screening hits, Rhot1 and VDAC3, led us to identify Kir7.1, a plasma membrane-localized K+ channel, as a key determinant of pigmentation. Integrating cellular, molecular, ultrastructural, and microscopy approaches, we demonstrate functional crosstalk between the hits and Kir7.1 channel activity. Mechanistically, Kir7.1 promotes the canonical cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) pathway, establishing this channel as a molecular node that couples K+ dynamics to the classical melanogenic pathway. Notably, Kir7.1 is differentially expressed in skin pigmentary disorders such as vitiligo and melasma, highlighting its therapeutic potential. Taken together, our findings establish Kir7.1 as an important regulator of skin pigmentation and reveal an unanticipated connection between K+ homeostasis, mitochondrial Ca2+ handling toolkit, and cAMP-dependent melanogenesis. This work provides a foundation for exploring K+ signaling as a potential therapeutic avenue for human pigmentary disorders.
